- btw-pull-request: Commits unrelated files to a clean PR without disrupting the current branch. Creates a temporary worktree off the base branch, copies specified files in, commits, pushes, and optionally opens a PR — then cleans up. Use when you have changes (README updates, config fixes, env templates, CI tweaks) that should land independently of the feature branch you're working on. Trigger when the user says "push this to a clean branch", "make a separate PR for this", "btw PR", or when you notice unrelated changes mixed into feature work that should be split out.
- dispatching-parallel-agents: Use when facing 2+ independent tasks that can be worked on without shared state or sequential dependencies
- frontend-design: Create distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces with high design quality. Use this skill when the user asks to build web components, pages, artifacts, posters, or applications (examples include websites, landing pages, dashboards, React components, HTML/CSS layouts, or when styling/beautifying any web UI). Generates creative, polished code and UI design that avoids generic AI aesthetics.
- initialize: Installs this harness's skills into a project by writing or updating AGENTS.md and/or CLAUDE.md with a skills reference and canonical workflow. Run this when setting up a new project, onboarding a repo to the spec→plan→TDD→verify→simplify→review→learn workflow, or when a project's context files are missing or don't reference these skills. Trigger when the user says "initialize this project", "set up AGENTS.md", "set up CLAUDE.md", "install skills", "onboard this repo", or "add skills to this project".
- learn-from-mistakes: Runs before and after human sign-off on a step. Logs human corrections, missed cases, and implementation holes for pattern tracking. Does not fix anything — the goal is to accumulate insight over time. When the same class of mistake occurs 3 or more times, surfaces a concrete suggestion to update AGENTS.md or an existing skill. Trigger after automated steps complete (pre-human) and again after human sign-off (post-human). Also trigger when the user says "log what went wrong", "retrospective", "what did we miss", or "learn from this".
- next-react-boot: Scaffold a Next.js 16 / React 19 / TypeScript / Tailwind CSS v4 frontend from scratch. Trigger when the user asks to bootstrap, scaffold, or create a new frontend, Next.js app, or React project. Also trigger when the user says "boot frontend", "new frontend", "create frontend", or "scaffold frontend".
- plan: Creates a structured implementation plan from a problem spec, breaking work into independently testable steps with dependency tracking and a living status dashboard. ONLY trigger this skill when a problem spec already exists at docs/<feature>/spec.md — if no spec is present, simpler ad-hoc planning suffices and this skill should not be used. Trigger on: "make a plan", "plan this out", "how should we implement this", "create an implementation plan", "break this into tasks", "what order should we build this in" — but only when a spec.md exists. If the user asks to plan something and there is no spec, tell them to run /problem-spec first.
- pr-interactive-walkthrough: Guides an interactive, file-by-file PR walkthrough in run order (startup then request path). Accepts two commit hashes to diff a specific range, or defaults to staged/branch diff. At the start, asks whether to use code snippets per file or summaries-only; skips tests, Markdown, and shell scripts by default; pauses after every question and after each file’s restate/walk-through prompt—never bundling the next file or §3 assessment with a pending question; ends with a calibrated understanding assessment (repo-hygiene files excluded from rubric) and follow-up questions for low-understanding areas. Use when the user asks for a PR walkthrough, to go through a PR together, file-by-file review, to check their understanding of a branch, or when the plan dashboard’s Understand column needs to be updated.
- problem-spec: First step for solving any complex coding problem. Defines what is and is not being solved, identifies all existing interfaces and contracts touched, and produces a structured spec doc. Trigger this skill whenever a user asks to build, implement, add, or solve something non-trivial. Do NOT trigger for small changes, refactors of a single function, or bug fixes. If there is any doubt about whether the problem is complex enough to warrant a spec, trigger it anyway — it is much cheaper to over-spec than to under-spec.
- refactor: Restructures existing code for modularity and clarity by actively applying Martin Fowler's refactoring catalog. Distinct from `/simplify` — refactor is invasive and assumes the user wants the structure changed, while simplify is conservative and biased toward silence. Trigger when the user says "refactor this", "make this more modular", "this file is too big", "split this up", "extract X out of Y", "this needs restructuring", or asks for Fowler-style moves on existing code. Do NOT trigger as part of the per-step workflow — refactor is an explicit, user-invoked operation, not a workflow stage.
- review: Reviews staged changes or a branch diff for bugs, missed edge cases, and unhandled error conditions. Runs three parallel reviewers — standard correctness, exhaustive path tracing, and adversarial — then merges findings and reports reviewer validity. Trigger when the user says "review this", "check for bugs", "what did I miss", "look for edge cases", or when the plan dashboard's Review column needs to be updated.
- simplify: Reviews staged changes or a branch diff and simplifies the code following XP Simple Design, Clean Code, and Martin Fowler refactoring principles. Applies clear improvements directly and suggests uncertain ones for human review. Biases toward silence — if a change isn't clearly better, don't make it or suggest it. Trigger when the user says "simplify", "clean this up", "refactor this", "is this the simplest solution", or when invoked as a subagent after staging and before committing. Also trigger when the plan dashboard's Simplify column needs to be updated.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- systematic-debugging: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
- verify: Runs end-to-end verification of implemented code against a live system. For APIs, fires real curl requests. For web UIs, runs browser automation. Reports what passed, what failed, and what could not be verified. Returns "verification incomplete" when the system cannot be reached or the verification cannot be run — this is distinct from a failure. Trigger when the user says "verify this", "test this end to end", "run the E2E", "check it works", or when the plan dashboard's LLM Verify column needs to be updated.
- problem-spec: First step for solving any complex coding problem. Defines what is and is not being solved, identifies all existing interfaces and contracts touched, and produces a structured spec doc. Trigger this skill whenever a user asks to build, implement, add, or solve something non-trivial. Do NOT trigger for small changes, refactors of a single function, or bug fixes. If there is any doubt about whether the problem is complex enough to warrant a spec, trigger it anyway — it is much cheaper to over-spec than to under-spec.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

> "Don't assume. Don't hide confusion. Surface tradeoffs."

Core practice:
- State your assumptions explicitly
- If uncertain, ask clarifying questions before implementing
- Present multiple interpretations when ambiguity exists
- Acknowledge simpler alternatives upfront

**Example anti-pattern:** When asked to "export user data," an LLM typically assumes all users without questioning privacy implications, file location, or field selection. Instead: ask scope, format, field selection, volume considerations upfront.

#### **Principle 2: Simplicity First**

> "Minimum code that solves the problem. Nothing speculative."

Core practice:
- Avoid speculative features (things not in the requirement)
- Don't add unnecessary abstractions or design patterns prematurely
- Don't implement unasked-for flexibility or error handling for improbable scenarios
- If substantial code reduction is possible through refactoring, do it; otherwise leave it

**Example anti-pattern:** A request to "calculate discount" doesn't need abstract base classes, strategy patterns, or configuration dataclasses. Start simple:
```python
def calculate_discount(amount: float, percent: float) -> float:
    return amount * (1 - percent / 100)
```
Only refactor when actual requirements demand it.

#### **Principle 3: Surgical Changes**

> "Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess."

Core practice:
- Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting
- Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently
- Remove only code your changes have made obsolete (imports, variables)
- Do NOT remove pre-existing dead code unrelated to your change
- Don't refactor while fixing bugs; fix first, refactor separately

**Example anti-pattern:** When fixing "empty emails crash the validator," resist the urge to reformat quotes, add type hints, or rewrite docstrings. Change only the specific lines addressing that bug.

#### **Principle 4: Goal-Driven Execution**

> "Convert abstract tasks into verifiable success criteria with specific checkpoints."

Core practice:
- Transform vague goals like "make it work" into measurable criteria
- Write tests that fail, then make them pass
- Create brief multi-step plans with verification checkpoints at each stage
- Break multi-step work into independently testable stages

**Example:** Rather than vague plan "review and improve code," specify:
1. Write test reproducing the bug
2. Implement fix
3. Verify test passes
4. Confirm no regressions

- How the agent **structures code** (minimal, simple, surgical)

- How the agent **approaches modifications** (surgical, not refactoring-happy)
- How the agent **validates work** (goal-driven with checkpoints)

What it does NOT affect:
- How the agent **talks to you** (no personality/tone changes)
- Output verbosity or friendliness
- Explanatory style or communication patterns

This is a **decision-making and implementation framework**, not a style guide for prose or personality. It says "write simpler code" and "ask questions before coding," not "be brief when talking" or "adopt Karpathy's writing voice."

#### **Hook 1: `caveman-activate.js` (SessionStart)**
**When:** Fires at the beginning of every Claude Code session
**What it does:**
1. Reads current mode from flag file at `~/.claude/.caveman-active`
2. Fetches the authoritative ruleset from `skills/caveman/SKILL.md` (or hardcoded fallback)
3. **Filters ruleset by intensity level** (lite/full/ultra/wenyan variant)
4. Injects filtered rules as **system context** to the model on every turn

const ruleset = loadRuleset(); // reads SKILL.md or uses fallback
const filtered = filterByLevel(ruleset, mode); // e.g., full mode strips articles
// Then emits context to Claude's SessionStart hook
```

- File size cap (64 bytes) to prevent exfiltration
- Silent fail on all filesystem errors (never blocks session)
- VALID_MODES whitelist prevents injection

#### **Hook 2: `caveman-mode-tracker.js` (UserPromptSubmit)**

3. **Updates mode state** by writing to `~/.claude/.caveman-active` flag file
4. For one-shot commands (`/caveman-commit`), **saves previous mode**, executes one-shot, then **restores previous mode**

be brief
less tokens
talk like caveman
// ... and ~20 more natural language patterns

**Deactivation patterns:**

disable caveman

- Prose modes (lite/full/ultra/wenyan) persist across turns
- Independent modes (commit/review/compress) are one-shot with auto-restore
- Per-turn reinforcement emits mode reminder to prevent model drift when multiple plugins compete for attention

#### **Hook 3: `caveman-statusline.sh` (statusline badge)**

  - Pull requests (normal prose)

- Modify coding standards or linter rules
- Change the model's code generation patterns
- Add pre-commit hooks or AST transforms

- Applies tone transformation to the **assistant's explanatory text**
- Leaves code blocks, commits, and PRs in **normal prose** (untouched)
- Preserves all technical terms, error messages, and command outputs exactly

[code block - unchanged]
```

The code output is identical; only the narration is compressed.

## Summary

Caveman is a **sophisticated, multi-agent tone-compression plugin** that:
- **Reduces output tokens by ~65%** through terse caveman-dialect speech
- **Injects tone via three Claude Code hooks** (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, statusline badge)

<result>Perfect! Now let me compile all this information into a structured technical breakdown. Based on my research, here's what I've discovered:

---

## Ponytail Technical Breakdown

### 1. **What It Does**

Ponytail is a **tone/personality plugin for AI coding agents** that enforces a "lazy senior developer" philosophy. It transforms agent behavior to prioritize **minimal, efficient code generation** by applying a hierarchical decision ladder *before* code is written.

**Philosophy**: "The best code is the code you never wrote." — Lazy means **efficient, not careless**.

**Impact Target**: It injects tone into **both user prompts and system instructions**, influencing the model's approach to code generation and problem-solving.

**Personality**: Adopts the archetype of a lazy senior developer who "says nothing, writes one line, it works" — emphasizing reuse, deletion over addition, and ruthless elimination of unnecessary code.

---

### 2. **File/Directory Structure**

```
ponytail/
├── .agents/                    # Hermes Agent plugin
│   ├── plugins/
│   ├── rules/                 # Agent-specific rules
├── .claude-plugin/            # Claude Code plugin (settings.json, hooks)
├── .clinerules/               # Cline editor rules
├── .codex-plugin/             # Codex plugin
├── .cursor/rules/             # Cursor editor rules
├── .devin-plugin/             # Devin CLI plugin
├── .github/
│   ├── FUNDING.yml
│   ├── copilot-instructions.md  # GitHub Copilot integration
├── .kiro/steering/            # Kiro agent steering rules
├── .opencode/
│   ├── plugins/ponytail.mjs    # OpenCode plugin implementation
├── .openclaw/                  # OpenClaw plugin
├── .qoder/
│   ├── rules/ponytail.md
│   └── plugin/
├── .windsurf/rules/           # Windsurf editor rules
├── pi-extension/
│   └── index.js               # Pi agent extension (session state mgmt)
├── ponytail-mcp/              # Model Context Protocol server
│   └── index.js               # MCP implementation (prompts + tools)
├── scripts/
│   └── check-rule-copies.js   # Validates rule consistency across platforms
├── skills/                    # Slash command implementations
├── benchmarks/results/        # Performance metrics (54% LOC reduction proven)
├── commands/                  # Command definitions
├── docs/                      # Documentation
├── examples/                  # Usage examples
├── hooks/                     # Hook implementations
├── tests/                     # Test suite
├── AGENTS.md                  # Main rule source document
├── plugin.yaml                # Hermes plugin metadata
├── package.json               # npm package config
├── opencode.json              # OpenCode plugin config
├── gemini-extension.json      # Gemini CLI extension
├── after-install.md           # Installation & setup guide
├── README.md                  # Main documentation
└── LICENSE (MIT)
```

**Key structural patterns**:
- **Rules are canonicalized**: `AGENTS.md` is the single source of truth; a script (`check-rule-copies.js`) ensures all platform-specific rule files stay synchronized
- **Multi-platform support**: Separate configuration for each agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, Windsurf, Codex, Devin, Kiro, OpenCode, Qoder, Pi, Gemini, etc.)
- **Two injection approaches**:
  - **Rules files** (.md) for direct prompt injection (Cursor, Windsurf, Cline)
  - **Plugins** (.yaml, .mjs, .js) with hooks for hook-based injection (Claude Code, OpenCode, Pi, MCP)

---

### 3. **Hook Mechanism — How It Injects Tone**

Ponytail uses **multiple injection strategies** depending on the agent platform:

#### **A. Claude Code / Hermes Plugin Hooks**

From `plugin.yaml`:
```yaml
name: ponytail
version: 4.8.4
provides_hooks:
  - pre_llm_call
  - pre_gateway_dispatch
provides_commands:
  - ponytail
  - ponytail-review
  - ponytail-audit
  - ponytail-debt
  - ponytail-gain
  - ponytail-help
```

**Hooks Used**:
- **`pre_llm_call`**: Injects ponytail instructions into the system prompt before the LLM is called
- **`pre_gateway_dispatch`**: Intercepts requests before gateway processing

#### **B. OpenCode Plugin System** (`ponytail.mjs`)

Hook mechanism via OpenCode's plugin API:
```
experimental.chat.system.transform:
  - Appends ponytail instructions to system prompt each turn
  - Respects mode setting (off disables injection)
  - Persists mode state to .ponytail-active file

command.execute.before:
  - Intercepts /ponytail command
  - Parses mode argument (lite/full/ultra/off)
  - Persists mode choice
```

#### **C. Pi Agent Extension** (`pi-extension/index.js`)

Session-based hook mechanism:
```
Events monitored:
  - Session initialization: Loads persisted mode settings
  - Pre-agent-start: Injects mode-specific instructions into system prompt
  - Agent startup/shutdown: Toggles status indicator
  - User input: Detects deactivation commands

Mode resolution:
  - Retrieves current mode from session history
  - Falls back to default if needed
  - Maintains local state variables for mode, status, context
```

#### **D. MCP Server** (`ponytail-mcp/index.js`)

Model Context Protocol integration (two interfaces):
```
Prompt Registration:
  - Registers prompt called "ponytail"
  - Accepts optional 'mode' parameter (lite, full, ultra)
  - Returns instructions as user message

Tool Registration:
  - Tool "ponytail_instructions"
  - Provides ruleset programmatically
  - Returns structured output (mode + instruction text)
  - Marked as read-only, closed-world

Shared functions:
  - resolveMode(): Normalizes mode parameter
  - buildInstructions(): Generates actual guidance text per mode
```

#### **E. Editor Integration** (Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Qoder, Kiro)

**No hooks** — uses direct `.md` rules files:
- `.cursor/rules/ponytail.md`
- `.windsurf/rules/ponytail.md`
- `.clinerules/ponytail.md`
- `.qoder/rules/ponytail.md`
- `.kiro/steering/ponytail.md`

These are injected by the editor's native rules system (no explicit hook configuration needed).

---

### 4. **Prompt/Instruction Content — Actual Tone Text**

The core instructions appear consistently across all platform variants. Here's the complete decision ladder and philosophy:

#### **The Decision Ladder** (7 rungs, stop at first match):

```
1. Does this need to be built at all? (YAGNI principle)
2. Does it already exist in this codebase? → Reuse existing helpers/patterns
3. Does the standard library already do this?
4. Does a native platform feature cover it?
5. Does an already-installed dependency solve it?
6. Can this be one line?
7. Only then: Write the minimum code that works
```

#### **Full Instruction Set** (Canonical text from `.clinerules/ponytail.md` and others):

```
You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. 
The best code is the code never written.

BEFORE CODING, address this ladder. Stop at the first rung that applies:

1. Is it necessary? Apply YAGNI principle
2. Already exists here? Reuse existing helpers/patterns
3. Standard library covers it? Use built-in functionality
4. Native platform feature? Leverage it
5. Dependency installed? Use existing packages
6. One-liner solution? Keep it minimal
7. Only then: Write minimal working code

CORE PRINCIPLES

What to avoid:
  - Unrequested abstractions
  - New dependencies when avoidable
  - Unnecessary boilerplate
  - Deletion preferred over addition
  - Simplicity over cleverness

What matters:
  - Full problem comprehension before coding
  - Input validation at trust boundaries
  - Error handling preventing data loss
  - Security and accessibility
  - Hardware calibration realities
  - Explicit requirements

QUALITY STANDARDS

Bug fixes: Address root causes, not symptoms. Fix shared functions 
once rather than patching individual call sites.

Deliberate shortcuts: Mark known trade-offs with `ponytail:` comments 
naming limitations and upgrade paths.

Testing: Non-trivial logic requires one small runnable check—no frameworks 
needed; trivial one-liners skip tests.
```

#### **By Intensity Mode**:

Ponytail supports **4 modes** with varying strictness:
- **`lite`**: Core principles only, minimal enforcement
- **`full`** (default): Complete decision ladder + all guardrails
- **`ultra`**: Aggressive minimalism, maximum reuse pressure
- **`off`**: Disables the plugin entirely

The actual instruction text adapts per mode (buildInstructions() generates mode-specific text).

---

### 5. **Installation Methods**

#### **Claude Code (Plugin Marketplace)**
```bash
/plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail
/plugin install ponytail@ponytail
```

Then enable:
```bash
hermes plugins enable ponytail
```

#### **Cursor / Windsurf / Cline / VS Code / JetBrains**
Copy the appropriate rules file to your project:
- Cursor: `.cursor/rules/ponytail.md` → `.cursor/rules/`
- Windsurf: `.windsurf/rules/ponytail.md` → `.windsurf/rules/`
- Cline: `.clinerules/ponytail.md` → `.clinerules/`

#### **OpenCode**
```json
{
  "plugin": ["@dietrichgebert/ponytail"]
}
```

Or: `opencode.json` → Add plugin reference

#### **Pi Agent Harness**
```bash
pi install git:github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail
```

#### **GitHub Copilot CLI**
```bash
copilot plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail
copilot plugin install ponytail@ponytail
```

#### **Other Platforms**
- **Qoder**: Copy `.qoder/rules/ponytail.md`
- **Devin CLI**: `devin plugins install DietrichGebert/ponytail`
- **Gemini CLI**: `gemini extensions install https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail`
- **Kiro**: `.kiro/steering/ponytail.md`

#### **Configuration**
Default mode can be set via:
- **Environment**: `PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE=lite|full|ultra|off`
- **Config file**: `~/.config/ponytail/config.json` with `defaultMode` field
- **Command**: `/ponytail [lite|full|ultra|off]`

---

### 6. **Slash Commands (Plugin Features)**

Available as both commands and callable skills:

| Command | Function |
|---------|----------|
| `/ponytail [lite\|full\|ultra\|off]` | Adjust intensity level, check status |
| `/ponytail-review` | Identifies over-engineering in current diff |
| `/ponytail-audit` | Scans entire repository for unnecessary complexity |
| `/ponytail-debt` | Catalogs deferred optimizations for later refactoring |
| `/ponytail-gain` | Displays benchmark performance improvements |
| `/ponytail-help` | Reference guide for all commands |

These are implemented in the `skills/` directory and callable programmatically via `ponytail:<skill-name>` in multi-agent workflows.

---

### 7. **Coding-Standards Injection — Pre-Code vs. Post-Code**

Ponytail injects instructions **BEFORE code generation** — not post-processing:

**Injection Point**: System prompt / LLM context before the model generates code

**Mechanism**: The ladder is presented *as part of the system message*, so the model evaluates necessity, reuse, and alternatives **before** writing a single line.

**NOT applied post-generation**: No linter, no rewriting pass. The instruction shapes decision-making during generation.

**Marked Code**: Shortcuts/known limitations are marked with `ponytail:` comments in the generated code itself:
```python
# ponytail: O(n²) scan but dataset < 1000 rows, safe for now
# upgrade path: add index if performance needed
```

---

### 8. **Safety Guarantees** (Non-Negotiable)

The plugin **never optimizes away**:
- **Trust boundary validation**: Input validation at system/user boundaries
- **Data loss prevention**: Error handling that prevents data loss
- **Security practices**: No weakening of crypto, auth, or trust checks
- **Accessibility standards**: WCAG compliance never sacrificed
- **Explicitly requested features**: If the user asked for it, the ladder doesn't apply

These are **invariant phrases** checked by the `check-rule-copies.js` validation script to prevent accidental regression.

---

### 9. **Performance Claims (Benchmarked)**

Real-world testing on `tiangolo/full-stack-fastapi-template` (FastAPI + React):

| Metric | Reduction |
|--------|-----------|
| **Lines of Code** | −54% (mean) |
| **Token Usage** | −22% |
| **Cost** | −20% |
| **Execution Time** | −27% |
| **Safety Rating** | 100% (security validation preserved) |

**High-impact areas** (60–94% reduction): Date pickers, form components, UI wrappers
**Minimal-code tasks** (convergence): Backend CRUD, already-lean code

---

### 10. **Key Implementation Files** (Summary)

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `AGENTS.md` | Canonical rule source (single source of truth) |
| `plugin.yaml` | Hermes plugin metadata & hook declarations |
| `.claude-plugin/settings.json` | Claude Code plugin configuration |
| `ponytail-mcp/index.js` | MCP server (prompt + tool injection) |
| `.opencode/plugins/ponytail.mjs` | OpenCode plugin with system prompt transform hook |
| `pi-extension/index.js` | Pi agent session-based injection |
| `scripts/check-rule-copies.js` | Validates rule consistency across platforms |
| `.cursor/rules/ponytail.md` | Cursor editor rules (canonical copy) |
| `.windsurf/rules/ponytail.md` | Windsurf editor rules |
| `.clinerules/ponytail.md` | Cline editor rules |
| `skills/ponytail/skill.md` | Skill implementation for slash commands |

---

### 11. **Architecture Patterns to Build Similar**

If you're building something similar:

1. **Canonicalize rules in one file** (AGENTS.md) + validation script to keep copies in sync
2. **Support multiple hook mechanisms**:
   - System prompt transformation (most universal)
   - Pre-LLM-call hooks (if platform supports)
   - MCP server (for agents without plugin hooks)
   - Editor rules files (for IDE integration)
3. **Implement mode-switching** (lite/full/ultra/off) with persistent state
4. **Protect safety invariants** via phrase-checking in tests/CI
5. **Provide slash commands** for runtime control (mode switching, auditing)
6. **Mark intentional optimizations** in code comments (upgrade paths)
7. **Benchmark real agent sessions** (not single-shot LLM calls) to validate claims

---

This completes the technical breakdown of Ponytail. The core innovation is **pre-generation tone injection via a decision ladder**, combined with **multi-platform support** through canonical rules, platform-agnostic MCP, and editor-native rules files.</result>

repo — the skills available, the canonical workflow, and behavioral rules accumulated from

---

## Nested AGENTS.md

Before starting any task, check whether an AGENTS.md exists in the directory you're working

<!-- nested-agents-index -->

If you create work in a subdirectory that would benefit from persistent local conventions,

---

For any non-trivial feature, work proceeds in this order. Do not skip steps — each one is a

```
/initialize     →  write or update AGENTS.md in a target project

    /review-comprehensive →  comprehensive correctness check; produces docs/reviews/<branch>-<date>.md

```

Failures in `/verify`, `/clean-code`, or `/review-comprehensive` require fixes or a plan update

| pr-interactive-walkthrough | `/pr-interactive-walkthrough` | File-by-file code walkthrough with understanding assessment |
| frontend-design | `/frontend-design` | Build distinctive, production-grade frontend UI |
| systematic-debugging | `/systematic-debugging` | Root-cause-first 4-phase debugging process |
| dispatching-parallel-agents | `/dispatching-parallel-agents` | Split independent tasks across parallel subagents |

Skills live in `skills/`. Each skill directory contains a `SKILL.md` and optionally
`sub-skills/`, `evals/`, and supporting scripts.

---

## Skill Routing

When the user makes a request, route it through this table before responding. The goal is

| If the user says... | Invoke |

# Tone + Coding Standards Plugin for the Harness

## Context

Caveman, Ponytail, and Karpathy-skills are all "influence-the-agent" plugins for Claude Code.
We researched all three (four parallel agents) to find the shared architecture and fold the good
parts into this harness. The goal: define a **conversation tone** and **general coding practices**
once, in `AGENTS.md`, and inject them into every session via hooks — tone always, coding standards
only when the prompt is a coding request.

### What the three reference repos actually are

| Repo | Concern | Injection | Modes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Caveman** | *Output tone only* — terse "caveman speak", ~65% fewer tokens. Never touches code. | SessionStart loads ruleset; UserPromptSubmit reinforces per-turn + tracks mode via flag file; statusline badge. | off/lite/full/ultra |
| **Ponytail** | *Coding practices* injected **before code** — "lazy senior dev" decision ladder (YAGNI → reuse → stdlib → one-line) with hard safety invariants never optimized away. | System-prompt transform / pre_llm_call; canonical `AGENTS.md` + sync-check script. | off/lite/full/ultra |
| **Karpathy** | *Coding practices* — 4 principles: think before coding, simplicity first, surgical changes, goal-driven execution. | Skill / plugin / Cursor `alwaysApply` rules. | n/a |

### The shared architecture (the overlap)

1. **One canonical source file** → copied/synced across platforms.
2. **Injected into context via hooks** (only SessionStart + UserPromptSubmit actually add text to
   the model's context — Stop/PostToolUse/SessionEnd cannot; "inject on all hooks" resolves to those two).
3. **Optional intensity modes** with persistent flag-file state.
4. **A slash command** for runtime control.
5. **Two cleanly separable concerns:** *tone* (Caveman) vs *coding standards* (Ponytail + Karpathy,
   which converge heavily on simplicity / reuse / surgical-change / verify).

### Decisions (locked with user)

- **Tone flavor:** Direct & terse (Caveman brevity, no gimmick).
- **Coding-standards injection:** UserPromptSubmit classifier — inject only on coding-intent prompts, before the model plans.
- **Modes:** Simple on/off (`HARNESS_TONE` env var). No intensity ladder / flag-file state machine yet.
- **Scope:** All projects — wire the harness now, then propagate via `install.sh` + `/initialize`.

---

## Architecture

Single source of truth = the harness's `tone/` text files. From there, two consumers:

```
tone/tone.md              ─┐   (1) SessionStart hook echoes tone rules once
tone/coding-standards.md  ─┼─► (2) UserPromptSubmit hook: always echoes a short tone
                           │       reminder; on coding-intent prompts also echoes standards
                           └─► written into each project's AGENTS.md by /initialize (human-visible,
                                   always loaded at session start)
```

- **Ambient presence** comes free from `AGENTS.md` (already read every session).
- **Hooks add** what `AGENTS.md` alone can't: per-turn tone reinforcement (prevents drift) and
  conditional standards injection targeted at coding prompts.
- **On/off:** hooks read `HARNESS_TONE`; if `off`, exit 0 silently. Existing `entire` hooks are untouched.

---

## Files to create

### 1. `tone/tone.md` — canonical direct-&-terse rules
Full ruleset (SessionStart) + a one-line `<!-- reminder -->` snippet the UserPromptSubmit hook emits per turn.
Draft content:
> Lead with the answer. Drop filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), pleasantries
> (sure/certainly/happy-to), and hedging. Fragments OK. Keep **all** technical substance, code
> blocks, and exact error strings verbatim. Applies to prose only — never to code, commit messages,
> or PR bodies. Revert to full sentences for security warnings, irreversible-action confirmations,
> and multi-step sequences where terseness risks misreading.

### 2. `tone/coding-standards.md` — distilled from Ponytail + Karpathy
The convergent standard (this is the "improve coding" deliverable):
1. **Think before coding** — state assumptions; ask when ambiguous; surface tradeoffs. *(Karpathy 1)*
2. **Necessity / YAGNI** — does this need to exist at all? *(Ponytail rung 1, Karpathy 2)*
3. **Reuse before writing** — existing helpers → stdlib → platform feature → installed dep → one line
   → only then new code. *(Ponytail ladder)*
4. **Simplicity** — minimum code that works; no speculative abstractions or unasked flexibility. *(both)*
5. **Surgical changes** — touch only what the task requires; match existing style; fix first, refactor
   separately; remove only code your change made obsolete. *(Karpathy 3, Ponytail root-cause)*
6. **Verify** — goal-driven; failing test first for non-trivial logic; checkpoints. *(Karpathy 4, Ponytail)*
7. **Safety invariants — never optimized away:** input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
   that prevents data loss, security, accessibility. *(Ponytail)*
8. **Mark deliberate shortcuts** with a `debt:` comment naming the limitation + upgrade path. *(Ponytail)*

Note in the file that these **complement** existing harness skills (`/clean-code`, `/refactor`,
`/review-comprehensive`) — they front-load the same values so the first draft is already close.

### 3. `hooks/tone-hooks.sh` — single dispatcher (mirrors `entire hooks claude-code <name>`)
```
tone-hooks.sh session-start        # if HARNESS_TONE != off: cat tone.md (full rules, once)
tone-hooks.sh user-prompt-submit   # if enabled: echo tone reminder;
                                   #   parse .prompt from stdin JSON; if it matches coding intent,
                                   #   also cat coding-standards.md
```
- Reads source files from `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/tone/` (harness local trial) with fallback to
  `$HOME/.claude/tone/` (global install). Silent-fail on any FS error (never blocks a session).
- Coding-intent regex (case-insensitive, bias toward inclusion — false positives just add context):
  `write|implement|add|create|build|fix|bug|refactor|function|class|method|endpoint|api|component|test|script|debug|compile|error`.
- Prompt arrives as JSON on stdin; extract `.prompt` (use `python3 -c` or `sed`/`grep` — no jq dependency).

## Files to modify

### 4. `AGENTS.md` (harness root) — add two anchored sections after "Behavioral Rules"
```
## Conversation Tone
<!-- tone -->        …direct & terse rules…        <!-- tone-end -->

## Coding Standards
<!-- coding-standards -->  …the 8 points above…  <!-- coding-standards-end -->
```
Anchors mirror the existing `<!-- learned-rules -->` pattern so `/initialize` can rewrite them idempotently.

### 5. `.claude/settings.json` (harness root) — add a second entry to two hook arrays
Alongside the existing `entire` entries (do not replace them):
- `SessionStart` → `{ "type": "command", "command": "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/hooks/tone-hooks.sh session-start" }`
- `UserPromptSubmit` → `{ "type": "command", "command": "$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/hooks/tone-hooks.sh user-prompt-submit" }`

This gives a **local trial inside the harness repo** before global rollout.

### 6. `install.sh` — propagate globally
- Copy `hooks/tone-hooks.sh` → `~/.claude/hooks/` and `tone/*.md` → `~/.claude/tone/`.
- Idempotently merge the two hook entries into `~/.claude/settings.json` (absolute path
  `$HOME/.claude/hooks/tone-hooks.sh`), backing up first — model the merge on caveman's `settings.js`
  (check-before-add, don't duplicate). This makes tone + standards fire in **all** sessions.

### 7. `skills/initialize/SKILL.md` — write the AGENTS.md sections into target projects
Extend the initializer so onboarding a project writes the `## Conversation Tone` and
`## Coding Standards` sections (with anchors) into that project's `AGENTS.md`, same as it already
does for the skills table and workflow.

---

## Out of scope (future)

- Intensity modes (lite/full/ultra) + flag-file state machine + `/tone` slash command + statusline badge.
  On/off first; the dispatcher is structured so a mode arg can be added later.
- PreToolUse-on-Edit/Write reinforcement (the "Both" option) — revisit if the prompt classifier misses cases.
- Multi-platform rule files (Cursor/Windsurf/etc.) — harness is Claude Code only.

---

## Verification

1. **Enable/disable:** `HARNESS_TONE=off` → run `echo '{"prompt":"fix the login bug"}' | hooks/tone-hooks.sh user-prompt-submit` → no output. Unset → tone reminder + standards appear.
2. **Classifier:** pipe a coding prompt (`"write a function to validate emails"`) → standards block present; pipe a non-coding prompt (`"what's the weather"`) → tone reminder only, no standards.
3. **SessionStart:** `hooks/tone-hooks.sh session-start` prints the full tone ruleset.
4. **Existing hooks intact:** confirm both the `entire` entry and the tone entry are present in each
   modified hook array (JSON valid; `entire` still fires).
5. **Live session (harness repo):** start a fresh session, give a coding request, confirm responses are
   terse in prose but code blocks / errors stay verbatim, and the model reuses existing helpers before
   writing new code.
6. **Global rollout:** run `install.sh`, confirm `~/.claude/settings.json` gained the entries and files
   landed in `~/.claude/hooks/` and `~/.claude/tone/`; start a session in an unrelated project and repeat check 5.

Here's the exact review-ready text for both sections — written to drop into `AGENTS.md` between the anchors verbatim. I've folded in your specifics (precise & concise, drop articles, pass errors/code directly, never restate prompts, no pleasantries, stay on task).

---

## `## Conversation Tone` (between `<!-- tone -->` … `<!-- tone-end -->`)

```markdown
Precise and concise. Every word earns its place.

- Lead with the answer. No preamble, no restating the user's request back to them.
- Drop articles (a/an/the) where meaning stays clear.
- Drop filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), hedging (maybe/perhaps/I think),
  and pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to/great question).
- Pass errors, stack traces, code, commands, and exact file paths through verbatim —
  never paraphrase, truncate, or "clean up" an error string.
- Fragments are fine. Short synonyms over long ones (big, not extensive).
- Stay on the task asked. No unrequested tangents, options, or scope.

Scope: applies to prose only. Never alter code blocks, commit messages, or PR bodies —
those stay in normal, complete form.

Revert to full, careful sentences for: security warnings, confirmation of irreversible
actions (deletes, force-push, migrations), and multi-step sequences where terseness risks
a misread. Resume terse after.
```

---

## `## Coding Standards` (between `<!-- coding-standards -->` … `<!-- coding-standards-end -->`)

```markdown
Apply before writing code, not after. Stop at the first rung that resolves the task.

1. Think first. State assumptions explicitly. If the request is ambiguous, ask before
   coding — do not guess and proceed. Surface tradeoffs and simpler alternatives up front.

2. Necessity (YAGNI). Does this need to be built at all? Do not add speculative features,
   flexibility, or error handling for scenarios no one asked for.

3. Reuse before writing. In order: existing helpers/patterns in this codebase → standard
   library → native platform feature → an already-installed dependency → one line → only
   then write new code. Do not add a dependency you can avoid.

4. Simplicity. Write the minimum code that solves the problem. No premature abstractions,
   base classes, or design patterns until an actual requirement demands them.

5. Surgical changes. Touch only what the task requires. Match the surrounding style even
   if you'd do it differently. Fix the bug first; refactor separately. Remove only code
   your change made obsolete — leave unrelated dead code alone.

6. Verify. For non-trivial logic, write the failing test first, then make it pass. Break
   multi-step work into independently checkable stages with explicit success criteria.

7. Safety invariants — never optimize these away, even under "make it minimal": input
   validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security
   (auth/crypto/secrets), and accessibility.

8. Mark deliberate shortcuts. When you knowingly take a tradeoff, leave a `debt:` comment
   naming the limitation and the upgrade path. Example:
   `// debt: O(n^2) scan, fine under ~1k rows; add an index if this grows`.

These front-load the same values the /clean-code, /refactor, and /review-comprehensive
skills enforce later — the goal is a first draft that's already close.
```

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# tone-hooks.sh — inject house tone + coding standards into Claude Code context.
#
# Source of truth: tone/tone.md and tone/coding-standards.md.
#   session-start        → inject tone (and coding standards) once, up front.
#   user-prompt-submit   → re-inject tone every turn; inject coding standards only when
#                          the prompt reads as a coding request.
#
# Disable entirely with HARNESS_TONE=off. Fails silently — never blocks a session.

event="${1:-}"

[ "${HARNESS_TONE:-on}" = "off" ] && exit 0

# Locate the source dir: project-local checkout first, then the global install.
tone_dir=""
for d in "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-}/tone" "$HOME/.claude/tone"; do
  if [ -f "$d/tone.md" ]; then tone_dir="$d"; break; fi
done
[ -z "$tone_dir" ] && exit 0

# Emit a source file with its anchor comment lines stripped.
emit() { sed '/^<!--/d' "$1" 2>/dev/null || true; }

standards="$tone_dir/coding-standards.md"

case "$event" in
  session-start)
    emit "$tone_dir/tone.md"
    [ -f "$standards" ] && { echo; emit "$standards"; }
    ;;
  user-prompt-submit)
    emit "$tone_dir/tone.md"
    payload="$(cat)"   # hook stdin: JSON containing the user's prompt
    # Bias toward inclusion — a false positive just adds context, a miss loses the standards.
    if printf '%s' "$payload" | grep -Eiq '\b(write|implement|add|create|build|fix|bug|refactor|function|class|method|endpoint|api|component|debug|compile|error|script|code)\b'; then
      [ -f "$standards" ] && { echo; emit "$standards"; }
    fi
    ;;
esac

exit 0

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# install.sh — install harness skills and context files at the user level
#
# Usage:
#   ./install.sh                          # default install into ~/.claude
#   ./install.sh --dir <path>             # alternate Claude Code dir (testing)
#   ./install.sh --with <skill>           # also install an optional skill
#                                         # (repeatable; e.g. --with next-react-boot)
#   ./install.sh --with all               # install every optional skill
#
# Skills land in <claude-dir>/skills/ and context files land in
# <claude-dir>/AGENTS.md and <claude-dir>/CLAUDE.md, so they apply to every
# project automatically.
#
# Optional skills are project bootstraps that only make sense in specific
# stacks. They are skipped by default. Request them explicitly with --with.

set -euo pipefail

HARNESS_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"

# ── optional skills ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Skipped by default; opt in with --with <name>.
OPTIONAL_SKILLS=(next-react-boot python-psql-boot)

# ── arg parsing ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
USER_CLAUDE_DIR="$HOME/.claude"
REQUESTED_OPTIONAL=()

while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
  case "$1" in
    --dir)
      USER_CLAUDE_DIR="$2"
      shift 2
      ;;
    --with)
      if [[ "$2" == "all" ]]; then
        REQUESTED_OPTIONAL=("${OPTIONAL_SKILLS[@]}")
      else
        REQUESTED_OPTIONAL+=("$2")
      fi
      shift 2
      ;;
    -h|--help)
      sed -n '2,16p' "$0"
      exit 0
      ;;
    *)
      printf 'unknown argument: %s\n' "$1" >&2
      printf 'see ./install.sh --help\n' >&2
      exit 1
      ;;
  esac
done

mkdir -p "$USER_CLAUDE_DIR"
USER_CLAUDE_DIR="$(cd "$USER_CLAUDE_DIR" && pwd)"
SKILLS_SRC="$HARNESS_DIR/skills"
SKILLS_DST="$USER_CLAUDE_DIR/skills"

# Validate any requested optional skills actually exist on disk.
for req in "${REQUESTED_OPTIONAL[@]+"${REQUESTED_OPTIONAL[@]}"}"; do
  if [[ ! -d "$SKILLS_SRC/$req" ]]; then
    printf 'requested optional skill not found: %s\n' "$req" >&2
    printf 'available optional skills: %s\n' "${OPTIONAL_SKILLS[*]}" >&2
    exit 1
  fi
done

# Helper: is this skill name an optional one?
is_optional() {
  local name="$1"
  local s
  for s in "${OPTIONAL_SKILLS[@]}"; do
    [[ "$s" == "$name" ]] && return 0
  done
  return 1
}

# Helper: was this optional skill requested?
is_requested() {
  local name="$1"
  local s
  for s in "${REQUESTED_OPTIONAL[@]+"${REQUESTED_OPTIONAL[@]}"}"; do
    [[ "$s" == "$name" ]] && return 0
  done
  return 1
}

# ── helpers ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

green()  { printf '\033[32m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
yellow() { printf '\033[33m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
bold()   { printf '\033[1m%s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }

# ── 1. copy skills ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

mkdir -p "$SKILLS_DST"

installed=()
updated=()
skipped=()

for skill_dir in "$SKILLS_SRC"/*/; do
  skill_name="$(basename "$skill_dir")"
  dst="$SKILLS_DST/$skill_name"

  if is_optional "$skill_name" && ! is_requested "$skill_name"; then
    skipped+=("$skill_name")
    continue
  fi

  if [[ -d "$dst" ]]; then
    rm -rf "$dst"
    cp -r "$skill_dir" "$dst"
    updated+=("$skill_name")
  else
    cp -r "$skill_dir" "$dst"
    installed+=("$skill_name")
  fi
done

# Prune skills that no longer exist in the harness source (handles renames + removals).
# An optional skill that wasn't requested is NOT pruned — it still exists in the source,
# so only genuinely deleted/renamed skills are removed.
removed=()
if [[ -d "$SKILLS_DST" ]]; then
  for dst_dir in "$SKILLS_DST"/*/; do
    [[ -d "$dst_dir" ]] || continue
    dst_name="$(basename "$dst_dir")"
    if [[ ! -d "$SKILLS_SRC/$dst_name" ]]; then
      rm -rf "$dst_dir"
      removed+=("$dst_name")
    fi
  done
fi

bold "Skills → $SKILLS_DST"
for s in "${installed[@]+"${installed[@]}"}"; do green  "  + $s"; done
for s in "${updated[@]+"${updated[@]}"}";    do yellow "  ↺ $s"; done
for s in "${removed[@]+"${removed[@]}"}";    do printf '  - %s (removed — no longer in harness)\n' "$s"; done
for s in "${skipped[@]+"${skipped[@]}"}";    do printf '  · %s (optional — request with --with %s)\n' "$s" "$s"; done

# ── 2. context files (AGENTS.md + CLAUDE.md) ─────────────────────────────────

HARNESS_REL="$(python3 -c "import os; print(os.path.relpath('$HARNESS_DIR', '$USER_CLAUDE_DIR'))" 2>/dev/null || echo "$HARNESS_DIR")"

skills_table() {
  cat <<EOF
| Skill | Invoke | SKILL.md |
|---|---|---|
| initialize | \`/initialize\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/initialize/SKILL.md) |
| problem-spec | \`/problem-spec\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/problem-spec/SKILL.md) |
| plan | \`/plan\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/plan/SKILL.md) |
| verify | \`/verify\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/verify/SKILL.md) |
| clean-code | \`/clean-code\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/clean-code/SKILL.md) |
| refactor | \`/refactor\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/refactor/SKILL.md) |
| review-comprehensive | \`/review-comprehensive\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/review-comprehensive/SKILL.md) |
| pr-interactive-walkthrough | \`/pr-interactive-walkthrough\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/pr-interactive-walkthrough/SKILL.md) |
| frontend-design | \`/frontend-design\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/frontend-design/SKILL.md) |
| systematic-debugging | \`/systematic-debugging\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/systematic-debugging/SKILL.md) |
| dispatching-parallel-agents | \`/dispatching-parallel-agents\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/dispatching-parallel-agents/SKILL.md) |
| skill-creator | \`/skill-creator\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/skill-creator/SKILL.md) |
| btw-pull-request | \`/btw-pull-request\` | [→]($HARNESS_REL/skills/btw-pull-request/skill.md) |
EOF
  for s in "${REQUESTED_OPTIONAL[@]+"${REQUESTED_OPTIONAL[@]}"}"; do
    printf '| %s | \`/%s\` | [→](%s/skills/%s/SKILL.md) |\n' "$s" "$s" "$HARNESS_REL" "$s"
  done
}

workflow_block() {
  printf '```\n'
  cat <<'EOF'
/initialize     →  write or update context files in a target project
/problem-spec   →  define the problem, produce docs/<feature>/spec.md
/plan           →  break into TDD chunks, produce docs/<feature>/plan.md

  For each step:
    write tests (red) → write code (green) → refactor → commit
    /verify              →  E2E check against live system
    /clean-code          →  clean up staged code
    /review-comprehensive →  comprehensive correctness and edge case check
    /pr-interactive-walkthrough  →  cognitive understanding check
    human                →  sign off
EOF
  printf '```\n'
}

# write_context_file <path> <title>
write_context_file() {
  local file="$1"
  local title="$2"   # e.g. "AGENTS.md" or "CLAUDE.md"
  local nested_label="$title"

  cat > "$file" <<EOF
# $title

Read by Claude at the start of every session. Links to skill files rather than
duplicating them. For full instructions, read the linked SKILL.md.

---

## Nested $nested_label

Check for $nested_label in subdirectories before starting work in them.

<!-- nested-agents-index -->
<!-- nested-agents-index-end -->

---

## Workflow

For non-trivial features, follow this order:

$(workflow_block)

---

## Skills

$(skills_table)

---

## Behavioral Rules

Rules added when a pattern of mistakes recurs 3+ times.

<!-- learned-rules -->
<!-- learned-rules-end -->
EOF
}

# update_context_file <path> <label>
update_context_file() {
  local file="$1"
  local label="$2"
  local changed=false

  if ! grep -q '## Skills' "$file"; then
    printf '\n---\n\n## Skills\n\n%s\n' "$(skills_table)" >> "$file"
    green "  + added ## Skills"
    changed=true
  fi

  if ! grep -q '## Workflow' "$file"; then
    printf '\n---\n\n## Workflow\n\nFor non-trivial features, follow this order:\n\n%s\n' "$(workflow_block)" >> "$file"
    green "  + added ## Workflow"
    changed=true
  fi

  if ! grep -q 'nested-agents-index' "$file"; then
    printf '\n---\n\n## Nested %s\n\nCheck for %s in subdirectories before starting work in them.\n\n<!-- nested-agents-index -->\n<!-- nested-agents-index-end -->\n' "$label" "$label" >> "$file"
    green "  + added nested index"
    changed=true
  fi

  if ! grep -q 'learned-rules' "$file"; then
    printf '\n---\n\n## Behavioral Rules\n\nRules added when a pattern of mistakes recurs 3+ times.\n\n<!-- learned-rules -->\n<!-- learned-rules-end -->\n' >> "$file"
    green "  + added learned-rules block"
    changed=true
  fi

  if $changed; then
    green "Updated $file"
  else
    yellow "$file already complete — no changes"
  fi
}

# ── process each context file ─────────────────────────────────────────────────

printf '\n'
bold "Context files → $USER_CLAUDE_DIR"

for fname in AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md; do
  target_file="$USER_CLAUDE_DIR/$fname"
  if [[ ! -f "$target_file" ]]; then
    write_context_file "$target_file" "$fname"
    green "Created $target_file"
  else
    update_context_file "$target_file" "$fname"
  fi
done

# ── 3. hooks + settings ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Install the verify-evidence PostToolUse hook: it blocks marking a step verified
# unless the verify report shows real evidence (curl / Playwright / DB check).

printf '\n'
bold "Hooks → $USER_CLAUDE_DIR/hooks"

HOOKS_DST="$USER_CLAUDE_DIR/hooks"
mkdir -p "$HOOKS_DST"
cp "$HARNESS_DIR/hooks/verify-evidence.sh" "$HOOKS_DST/verify-evidence.sh"
chmod +x "$HOOKS_DST/verify-evidence.sh"
green "  + verify-evidence.sh"

SETTINGS="$USER_CLAUDE_DIR/settings.json"
HOOK_CMD="$HOOKS_DST/verify-evidence.sh"

if command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  [[ -f "$SETTINGS" ]] || echo '{}' > "$SETTINGS"
  if jq -e --arg c "$HOOK_CMD" '[.hooks.PostToolUse[]?.hooks[]?.command] | index($c)' "$SETTINGS" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    yellow "  settings.json already registers the verify-evidence hook — no change"
  else
    tmp="$(mktemp)"
    jq --arg c "$HOOK_CMD" '
      .hooks.PostToolUse = ((.hooks.PostToolUse // []) + [
        { matcher: "Skill", hooks: [ { type: "command", command: $c } ] }
      ])' "$SETTINGS" > "$tmp" && mv "$tmp" "$SETTINGS"
    green "  + registered verify-evidence PostToolUse hook in settings.json"
  fi
else
  yellow "  jq not found — add this to $SETTINGS manually:"
  cat <<EOF
    "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [
      { "matcher": "Skill",
        "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "$HOOK_CMD" } ] } ] }
EOF
fi

# ── done ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

printf '\n'
bold "Done. Next steps:"
echo "  claude          # start a session in any project — skills are active"
echo "  /problem-spec   # begin your first feature"
printf '\n'
yellow "Note: skills and context are installed at the user level ($USER_CLAUDE_DIR)."
yellow "They apply to every project automatically. No per-repo install needed."

if [[ ${#skipped[@]} -gt 0 ]]; then
  printf '\n'
  bold "Optional skills available (not installed):"
  for s in "${skipped[@]}"; do
    echo "  ./install.sh --with $s"
  done
  echo "  ./install.sh --with all   # install everything"
fi

1	---
2	name: initialize
3	description: >
4	  Installs this harness's skills into a project by writing or updating AGENTS.md and/or
5	  CLAUDE.md with a skills reference and canonical workflow. Run this when setting up a new
6	  project, onboarding a repo to the spec→plan→TDD→verify→clean-code→review workflow, or
7	  when a project's context files are missing or don't reference these skills. Trigger when the
8	  user says "initialize this project", "set up AGENTS.md", "set up CLAUDE.md", "install
9	  skills", "onboard this repo", or "add skills to this project".
10	---
11	
12	# Initialize
13	
14	Install this harness's skills into a target project by writing or updating its context files.
15	
16	Claude Code reads **CLAUDE.md** for project context. Codex and other agents read **AGENTS.md**.
17	Both serve the same purpose — orient the AI in a new session. This skill writes whichever
18	file(s) the project needs.
19	
20	The goal is minimal files that link out to canonical skill files rather than duplicating their
21	contents. Less is more.
22	
23	## Step 1: Locate the harness
24	
25	The harness root is the directory containing `skills/`. Confirm the following exist:
26	
27	- `skills/problem-spec/SKILL.md`
28	- `skills/plan/SKILL.md`
29	- `skills/verify/SKILL.md`
30	- `skills/clean-code/SKILL.md`
31	- `skills/review-comprehensive/SKILL.md`
32	
33	Record the absolute path to the harness root. You'll use it to compute relative links.
34	
35	## Step 2: Identify the target project
36	
37	Usually the current working directory. If the user provided a path, use that.
38	
39	If ambiguous, ask: "Which directory should I initialize — this one (`<cwd>`), or somewhere
40	else?"
41	
42	## Step 3: Determine which files to write
43	
44	Check what exists at the target project root:
45	
46	| State | Action |
47	|---|---|
48	| Neither file exists | Create both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md |
49	| Only CLAUDE.md exists | Update CLAUDE.md; create AGENTS.md |
50	| Only AGENTS.md exists | Update AGENTS.md; create CLAUDE.md |
51	| Both exist | Update both |
52	
53	If the user explicitly said "only CLAUDE.md" or "only AGENTS.md", respect that and skip the
54	other.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## Content blocks
59	
60	Both files use the same four sections. Tailor the heading style to the file (CLAUDE.md can
61	use a friendlier intro; AGENTS.md is terse).
62	
63	### Nested context index
64	
65	```markdown
66	## Nested AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md
67	
68	Check for context files in subdirectories before starting work in them.
69	
70	<!-- nested-agents-index -->
71	<!-- nested-agents-index-end -->
72	```
73	
74	### Workflow
75	
76	```
77	/initialize     →  write or update context files in a target project
78	/problem-spec   →  define the problem, produce docs/<feature>/spec.md
79	/plan           →  break into TDD chunks, produce docs/<feature>/plan.md
80	
81	  For each step:
82	    write tests (red) → write code (green) → refactor → commit
83	    /verify              →  E2E check against live system
84	    /clean-code          →  clean up staged code
85	    /review-comprehensive →  comprehensive correctness and edge case check
86	    /pr-interactive-walkthrough  →  cognitive understanding check
87	    human                →  sign off
88	```
89	
90	### Skills table
91	
92	Replace `<harness-path>` with the actual relative or absolute path from the target project
93	to the harness root. Prefer relative paths when they share a common parent.
94	
95	```markdown
96	## Skills
97	
98	| Skill | Invoke | SKILL.md |
99	|---|---|---|
100	| initialize | `/initialize` | [→](<harness-path>/skills/initialize/SKILL.md) |
101	| problem-spec | `/problem-spec` | [→](<harness-path>/skills/problem-spec/SKILL.md) |
102	| plan | `/plan` | [→](<harness-path>/skills/plan/SKILL.md) |
103	| verify | `/verify` | [→](<harness-path>/skills/verify/SKILL.md) |
104	| clean-code | `/clean-code` | [→](<harness-path>/skills/clean-code/SKILL.md) |
105	| review-comprehensive | `/review-comprehensive` | [→](<harness-path>/skills/review-comprehensive/SKILL.md) |
106	```
107	
108	### Behavioral rules block
109	
110	```markdown
111	## Behavioral Rules
112	
113	Rules added when a pattern of mistakes recurs 3+ times.
114	
115	<!-- learned-rules -->
116	<!-- learned-rules-end -->
117	```
118

# Initialize

Install this harness's skills into a target project by writing or updating its context files.

Claude Code reads **CLAUDE.md** for project context. Codex and other agents read **AGENTS.md**.
Both serve the same purpose — orient the AI in a new session. This skill writes whichever
file(s) the project needs.

The goal is minimal files that link out to canonical skill files rather than duplicating their
contents. Less is more.

## Step 1: Locate the harness

The harness root is the directory containing `skills/`. Confirm the following exist:

- `skills/problem-spec/SKILL.md`
- `skills/plan/SKILL.md`
- `skills/verify/SKILL.md`
- `skills/clean-code/SKILL.md`
- `skills/review-comprehensive/SKILL.md`

Record the absolute path to the harness root. You'll use it to compute relative links.

## Step 2: Identify the target project

Usually the current working directory. If the user provided a path, use that.

If ambiguous, ask: "Which directory should I initialize — this one (`<cwd>`), or somewhere
else?"

## Step 3: Determine which files to write

Check what exists at the target project root:

| State | Action |
|---|---|
| Neither file exists | Create both CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md |
| Only CLAUDE.md exists | Update CLAUDE.md; create AGENTS.md |
| Only AGENTS.md exists | Update AGENTS.md; create CLAUDE.md |
| Both exist | Update both |

other.

---

use a friendlier intro; AGENTS.md is terse).

House voice for all prose. Source of truth: `tone/tone.md` (the SessionStart /
UserPromptSubmit hooks inject it every turn). Disable with `HARNESS_TONE=off`.

<!-- tone -->

Precise and concise.

- Lead with the answer. No preamble, no restating the user's request back to them.
- Drop articles (a/an/the) where meaning stays clear.
- Drop filler (just/really/basically/actually/simply), hedging (maybe/perhaps/I think),
  and pleasantries (sure/certainly/of course/happy to/great question).
- Be logically precise; use exact words for concepts. If unsure, raise it.
- Pass errors, stack traces, code, commands, and exact file paths through verbatim —
  never paraphrase, truncate, or "clean up" an error string.
- Fragments are fine. Short synonyms over long ones (big, not extensive).

For user questions:

- Always ask one question at a time. Handle all follow-ups before moving on to the next question.

Scope: applies to prose only. Never alter code blocks, commit messages, security warnings, error messages, or PR bodies —
those stay in normal, complete form.

UserPromptSubmit hook injects it when the prompt reads as a coding request).

<!-- coding-standards -->

Apply before writing code, not after. Stop at the first rung that resolves the task.

1. Think first. State assumptions explicitly. If the request is ambiguous, ask before
   coding — do not guess and proceed. Surface tradeoffs and simpler alternatives up front.

2. Necessity (YAGNI). Does this need to be built at all? Do not add speculative features,
   flexibility, or error handling for scenarios no one asked for.

3. Reuse before writing. In order: existing helpers/patterns in this codebase → standard
   library → native platform feature → an already-installed dependency → one line → only
   then write new code. Do not add a dependency you can avoid.

4. Simplicity. Write the minimum code that solves the problem. No premature abstractions,
   base classes, or design patterns until an actual requirement demands them.

5. Surgical changes. Touch only what the task requires. Match the surrounding style even
   if you'd do it differently. Fix the bug first; refactor separately. Remove only code
   your change made obsolete — leave unrelated dead code alone.

6. Verify. For non-trivial logic, write the failing test first, then make it pass. Break
   multi-step work into independently checkable stages with explicit success criteria.
   Trivial one-liners skip tests.

7. Safety invariants — never optimize these away, even under "make it minimal": input
   validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security
   (auth/crypto/secrets), and accessibility.

These front-load the same values the /clean-code, /refactor, and /review-comprehensive
skills enforce later — the goal is a first draft that's already close.

<!-- coding-standards-end -->

# AGENTS.md

This file is read by Claude at the start of every session. It describes how to work in this
repo — the skills available, the canonical workflow, and behavioral rules accumulated from
past mistakes. It does not repeat what is in Readme.md or the individual skill files.

---

## Nested AGENTS.md

Before starting any task, check whether an AGENTS.md exists in the directory you're working
in or any of its parent directories (up to this root). If one exists, read it — it contains
context specific to that part of the codebase. Known nested files:

<!-- nested-agents-index -->
<!-- Add entries here as nested AGENTS.md files are created, e.g.:             -->
<!-- - [skills/plan/AGENTS.md](skills/plan/AGENTS.md) — plan skill conventions -->
<!-- nested-agents-index-end -->

If you create work in a subdirectory that would benefit from persistent local conventions,
create an AGENTS.md there and link it in the index above.

---

## Canonical Workflow

For any non-trivial feature, work proceeds in this order. Do not skip steps — each one is a
skill that can be invoked explicitly.

```
/initialize     →  write or update AGENTS.md in a target project
/problem-spec   →  define the problem, produce docs/<feature>/spec.md
/plan           →  break into steps, produce docs/<feature>/plan.md + docs/<feature>/steps/<step-name>.md
                   (requires spec.md to exist)

  For each step:
    write tests (red) → write code (green) → refactor → commit
    /verify              →  E2E check against live system; produces docs/verify/<branch>-<date>.md
    /clean-code          →  clean up staged code; produces docs/simplify/<branch>-<date>.md
    /review-comprehensive →  comprehensive correctness check; produces docs/reviews/<branch>-<date>.md
    /pr-interactive-walkthrough  →  cognitive understanding check
    human                →  developer signs off
```

Failures in `/verify`, `/clean-code`, or `/review-comprehensive` require fixes or a plan update
before proceeding. The Human column in the plan dashboard cannot be marked ✅ while any prior
column is ❌.

---

## Skills Reference

Each skill has a full SKILL.md. This table is a quick reference only — read the SKILL.md
for complete instructions.

| Skill | Invoke | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| initialize | `/initialize` | Write or update AGENTS.md in a project with skills reference and workflow |
| problem-spec | `/problem-spec` | Define what is and isn't being solved; produce a spec doc |
| plan | `/plan` | Break a spec into testable TDD chunks with a status dashboard |
| verify | `/verify` | E2E verification — real curl or browser automation against a live system |
| clean-code | `/clean-code` | Apply clear improvements; suggest uncertain ones; never touch tests |
| refactor | `/refactor` | Restructure existing code with Fowler's catalog; Chesterton's Fence on every removal |
| review-comprehensive | `/review-comprehensive` | Comprehensive review — bugs, missed edge cases, unhandled errors; report only |
| pr-interactive-walkthrough | `/pr-interactive-walkthrough` | File-by-file code walkthrough with understanding assessment |
| frontend-design | `/frontend-design` | Build distinctive, production-grade frontend UI |
| systematic-debugging | `/systematic-debugging` | Root-cause-first 4-phase debugging process |
| dispatching-parallel-agents | `/dispatching-parallel-agents` | Split independent tasks across parallel subagents |

Skills live in `skills/`. Each skill directory contains a `SKILL.md` and optionally
`sub-skills/`, `evals/`, and supporting scripts.

---

## Skill Routing

When the user makes a request, route it through this table before responding. The goal is
to invoke the right skill instead of doing ad-hoc work that bypasses the workflow.

| If the user says... | Invoke |
|---|---|
| "build / add / implement / create [non-trivial feature]" | `/problem-spec` (then `/plan`) |
| "make a plan", "how should we build this", "break this into tasks" | `/plan` (requires spec.md to exist; if not, run `/problem-spec` first) |
| "set up AGENTS.md", "onboard this repo", "install the skills here" | `/initialize` |
| "verify this", "test it end to end", "check that it works", "run the e2e" | `/verify` |
| "simplify this", "clean this up", "is this the simplest version" | `/clean-code` |
| "refactor this", "make this more modular", "this file is too big", "extract X out of Y", "split this up", "reduce coupling" | `/refactor` |
| "review this", "find bugs", "what did I miss", "look for edge cases" | `/review-comprehensive` |
| "walk me through this PR", "explain this code", "do I understand this" | `/pr-interactive-walkthrough` |
| "debug this", "why is X failing", "find the root cause" | `/systematic-debugging` |
| "design this UI", "make this look good", "build the frontend for X" | `/frontend-design` |
| "split this work", "run these in parallel", "dispatch agents" | `/dispatching-parallel-agents` |
| "create a skill", "add a new skill", "improve this skill" | `/skill-creator` |

**Routing rules — read before invoking:**

1. **Bug fixes go to `/systematic-debugging`, not `/problem-spec`.** Specs are for new
   capabilities. If the user says "fix this bug" or "X is broken," skip the spec.
2. **`/plan` requires a spec.** If `docs/<feature>/spec.md` doesn't exist, refuse and run
   `/problem-spec` first. Do not improvise a plan from a verbal description.
3. **`/review-comprehensive` ≠ `/pr-interactive-walkthrough`.** Review hunts for bugs and edge
   cases. Walkthrough tests human comprehension. Both run per step; they are not interchangeable.
4. **`/clean-code` and `/review-comprehensive` have two run modes.** In *workflow mode* (running
   as part of a plan-driven step), the prior-step gate enforces order: Auto Tests → Verify →
   Clean Code → Comp Review. In *standalone mode* (running ad-hoc on staged changes, a PR, or a
   branch diff outside any plan), the gate is skipped — the caller is asking for a one-off pass.
   Don't try to bypass the gate in workflow mode; do feel free to run either skill directly when
   the work isn't tied to a plan.
5. **Don't run a skill as a list.** If you find yourself "summarizing what /clean-code would
   say" or "doing a quick mental review," stop and invoke the actual skill. The sub-skills
   and gates only fire when the skill runs.
6. **Trivial changes don't need the workflow.** A typo fix, a single-line CSS tweak, or a
   one-character rename can be done directly. Use judgment — when in doubt, route through
   the workflow rather than around it.

---

## Behavioral Rules

Rules added here when a pattern of mistakes recurs 3+ times. Starts empty.

<!-- learned-rules -->
<!-- learned-rules-end -->

---

## What This File Is Not

- Not a duplicate of Readme.md (see that for repo purpose)
- Not a directory listing (derive structure from the repo itself)
- Not a copy of individual SKILL.md files (read those directly)

# Tone hooks: inject house tone (every turn) + coding standards (on coding prompts).
TONE_HOOK="$HOOKS_DST/tone-hooks.sh"

register_tone_hook() {
  local evt="$1" cmd="$2" tmp
  if jq -e --arg e "$evt" --arg c "$cmd" '[.hooks[$e][]?.hooks[]?.command] | index($c)' "$SETTINGS" >/dev/null 2>&1; then

      ])' "$SETTINGS" > "$tmp" && mv "$tmp" "$SETTINGS"
    green "  + registered tone $evt hook in settings.json"
  fi
}

Hook's live — it injected into that very prompt. Now: independent toggles.

Design: two flag files (`.tone-off`, `.standards-off`) in a stable state dir, checked by the hook; a `toggle`/`status` subcommand in `tone-hooks.sh` owns the path logic; a `/tone` skill drives it. `HARNESS_TONE=off` stays as the master kill switch.

Rewriting the hook with the gating + subcommands:

input.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# tone-hooks.sh — inject house tone + coding standards into Claude Code context,
# and toggle each independently.
#
# Events (wired in settings.json):
#   session-start        → inject tone + coding standards once, up front.
#   user-prompt-submit   → re-inject tone; inject coding standards on coding prompts.
#
# Control:
#   tone-hooks.sh toggle tone on|off        enable/disable the tone
#   tone-hooks.sh toggle standards on|off   enable/disable the coding standards
#   tone-hooks.sh status                    show current state
#
# State lives in flag files under $HARNESS_TONE_STATE (default ~/.claude/tone), so a
# toggle persists across sessions and projects. HARNESS_TONE=off is a master kill switch
# for both; HARNESS_STANDARDS=off disables standards only. Fails silently — never blocks.

cmd="${1:-}"

STATE_DIR="${HARNESS_TONE_STATE:-$HOME/.claude/tone}"
TONE_OFF="$STATE_DIR/.tone-off"
STANDARDS_OFF="$STATE_DIR/.standards-off"

tone_enabled() {
  [ "${HARNESS_TONE:-on}" = "off" ] && return 1
  [ -f "$TONE_OFF" ] && return 1
  return 0
}

standards_enabled() {
  [ "${HARNESS_TONE:-on}" = "off" ] && return 1
  [ "${HARNESS_STANDARDS:-on}" = "off" ] && return 1
  [ -f "$STANDARDS_OFF" ] && return 1
  return 0
}

# Locate source files: project checkout first, then the global install.
find_tone_dir() {
  local d
  for d in "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR:-}/tone" "$HOME/.claude/tone"; do
    [ -f "$d/tone.md" ] && { printf '%s' "$d"; return 0; }
  done
  return 1
}

# Emit a source file with its anchor comment lines stripped.
emit() { sed '/^<!--/d' "$1" 2>/dev/null || true; }

case "$cmd" in
  session-start|user-prompt-submit)
    tone_dir="$(find_tone_dir)" || exit 0
    [ "$cmd" = "user-prompt-submit" ] && payload="$(cat)"

    tone_enabled && emit "$tone_dir/tone.md"

    if standards_enabled && [ -f "$tone_dir/coding-standards.md" ]; then
      if [ "$cmd" = "session-start" ]; then
        echo; emit "$tone_dir/coding-standards.md"
      # Bias toward inclusion — a false positive just adds context, a miss loses the standards.
      elif printf '%s' "$payload" | grep -Eiq '\b(write|implement|add|create|build|fix|bug|refactor|function|class|method|endpoint|api|component|debug|compile|error|script|code)\b'; then
        echo; emit "$tone_dir/coding-standards.md"
      fi
    fi
    ;;

  toggle)
    mkdir -p "$STATE_DIR" 2>/dev/null
    case "${2:-}:${3:-}" in
      tone:off)      : > "$TONE_OFF";       echo "tone: OFF" ;;
      tone:on)       rm -f "$TONE_OFF";      echo "tone: ON" ;;
      standards:off) : > "$STANDARDS_OFF";  echo "coding standards: OFF" ;;
      standards:on)  rm -f "$STANDARDS_OFF"; echo "coding standards: ON" ;;
      *) echo "usage: tone-hooks.sh toggle {tone|standards} {on|off}" >&2; exit 2 ;;
    esac
    ;;

  status)
    if tone_enabled;      then echo "tone: ON";            else echo "tone: OFF"; fi
    if standards_enabled; then echo "coding standards: ON"; else echo "coding standards: OFF"; fi
    [ "${HARNESS_TONE:-on}" = "off" ] && echo "(HARNESS_TONE=off — master kill switch active)"
    ;;
esac

exit 0
